title: Back and Forward in One Tab
statement:
Model the history of a single browser tab, the way the back and forward buttons work.

  • TabHistory(home) opens the tab on page home.
  • visit(url) goes from the current page to url. All forward history is thrown away, just as a real browser forgets the pages you went back from once you navigate somewhere new.
  • back(steps) moves back up to steps pages. If there are fewer pages behind you, stop at the first one. Return the page you end on.
  • forward(steps) moves forward up to steps pages, stopping at the newest one. Return the page you end on.

Tests are a list of operations; the first one creates the tab. The output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.why: Visiting d.io from b.io erases c.io, so forward(2) has nowhere to go and stays on d.io. back(5) stops at the first page.
A fresh tab has nothing behind it and nothing ahead of it.

constraints: 1 ≤ home.length, url.length ≤ 20, lowercase letters and dots
hints: Back and forward undo and redo each other. Which structure fits undo and redo?
Two stacks work: pages behind you and pages ahead of you. What does visit do to the stack of pages ahead?

Even simpler: one array, an index cur for the current page, and an index last for the newest valid page. visit writes at cur + 1 and sets last = cur + 1. back and forward just clamp cur between 0 and last.

explain.intuition:
History is a straight line of pages with you standing somewhere on it. Back and forward only move your position. visit is the only call that changes the line: it cuts off everything ahead of you and adds the new page.

So store the line in an array with two indexes: cur (where you are) and last (the newest page that still counts). back and forward are a clamp, O(1). visit writes the page at cur + 1, overwriting or appending, and sets last = cur + 1. Old entries beyond last may still sit in the array, but last stops you from reaching them, so nothing has to be deleted. This is the undo/redo model used by editors and by history.pushState.
steps: visit(url): cur++; write url at pages[cur] (append if the array is shorter); set last = cur.
pitfalls: Keeping forward history after a visit. In the first example, forward after visiting d.io must not bring back c.io.
Clamping forward to the array length instead of last. Stale pages past last are still in the array.
Returning nothing, or the old page, when the steps run past the end. The call still returns the page you end on.

solutions.title: Two stacks
solutions.idea: One stack for pages behind you (top = current page), one for pages ahead. Moving shifts pages between them; visit clears the forward stack.
solutions.time: O(steps) for back and forward, O(1) amortized for visit

solutions.title: One array with a cursor and an end marker
solutions.idea: Store the line of pages once. cur is your position, last is the newest valid page. visit overwrites at cur + 1 and moves last there.

followups: Add a method that returns the full list of pages reachable with back and forward right now. Which design makes that cheap?
Support many tabs, where opening a link in a new tab copies the history up to the current page. How do you avoid copying the whole array each time?
